title: Medial deep dorsal glycinergic interneurons as a target for improving locomotion following spinal cord injury
text:
This study will examine the function of a population of spinal deep dorsal inhibitory interneurons that inhibit
locomotor circuit interneurons, and the plasticity of afferent pathways to this population after spinal cord injury.
The findings from this proposal will reveal potential neurons and pathways to serve as therapeutic targets for the
restoration of locomotion after spinal cord injury.

title: Pathological Autoantibodies Contribute to Immune Suppression in Sepsis
text:
Mortality after sepsis is associated with suppression of the immune system and an increased risk of infection.
This research investigates a novel mechanism of immune suppression that is associated with critical illness,
namely antibodies against self-proteins in the immune system. Armed with this information, a new therapeutic
modality will be developed to preserve the immune system in patients with severe illnesses like sepsis.

title: Shining light on the mechanisms of primate gastrulation:  development of high-throughput, optogenetic tools for understanding embryonic development
text:
Despite its importance to the formation of the body plan, little is known about the mechanisms driving primate
gastrulation. We aim to create a high-throughput, three-dimensional model of the peri-implantation primate
embryo using chimpanzee induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) encapsulated in hydrogel droplets. By using a
microfluidic droplet sorter to control the number of cells and cell types in each droplet, we will investigate the
impact of cell number, cell type, and local tissue mechanics on model embryo structure and explore the role of
morphogen signaling dynamics on cell fate decisions via downstream optogenetic stimulation.

title: ZIP8-dependent Zinc Metabolic Regulation in Alveolar Progenitor Cell Aging and Fibrosis
text:
With rapid growth of aging population, the annual incidence of aging related lung diseases is increasing. Our
goal of this proposal is to test the hypothesis that ZIP8 deficiency in AEC2s which occurs with aging contributes
to dysfunction of AEC2s progenitor cells leading to lung aging and restoration the components in ZIP8 mediated
zinc metabolism may promote AEC2 renewal and slow down lung aging.

title: Molecular and cellular underpinnings of placental malaria
text: In the US, mosquito-borne infections during pregnancy, such as West Nile Virus, dengue fever and the rising incidence of locally transmitted malaria are significant health threats during fetal, neonatal, and later stages of life. The proposed study will investigate the impact of placental malaria on placenta function with the overarching aim of developing simple, cost-effective tools for the detection of placental infection during pregnancy. This study’s data, findings, and tools will significantly improve our understanding of the mechanisms underlying placental infections and will be directly available to US partners on this project and the American public health research community for exploitation to develop simple, fast, sensitive, and affordable diagnostics for other placenta infections in the US, e.g. CMV and toxoplasmosis.

title: Precision PET attenuation correction for combined PET/MR imaging of cardiac sarcoidosis
text:
The proposed research is relevant to the public health because the development of a high performance PET
radiotracer attenuation correction strategy for cardiac PET/MR exams has the potential to improve the strength
of research and clinical findings based on PET measurements. This will enable PET/MR to provide an accurate
diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy response monitoring of cardiac diseases.

title: Radiopaque 3D printed tissue engineered scaffolds for nerve generation
text:
Peripheral nerve injury represents a major healthcare burden worldwide, that often requires treatment with
implanted biomedical devices. By incorporating radiopaque tantalum oxide nanoparticles into devices, clinicians
will gain the ability to monitor healing, reducing delays to treatment that jeopardize patient outcomes.

title: Proliferative asymmetry in the neural stem cell lineage established by asymmetric cell division
text:
Tissues and organs are comprised of many different types of cells which are all made from stem cells. Failure to
make the proper number of cells can cause disease. The goal of this project is to understand how stem cells
produce the correct number of cells, in the hopes that this understanding can lead to new disease treatments.

title: Homeostatic plasticity mechanisms regulate behavior in vivo
text:
Modern neuroscience seeks to identify cellular plasticity mechanisms that act to keep brain activity in a healthy
range because when these processes fail, neurological disorders such as epilepsy and Alzheimer’s disease
may follow. Despite significant progress, how the brain uses these mechanisms to control circuit function and
behavior in realistic contexts for animals remains a major challenge. This proposal takes advantage of an
innovative model system that will uncover how neurons integrate stabilizing forms of plasticity to generate a
tractable behavior in a natural environment.

title: Dissecting the genetics and evolution of complex traits using whole-genome genealogies
text:
Correlations among mutations naturally arise and decay along the branches in an ancestral
recombination graph (ARG) due to mutation, coalescence, and recombination. Developing novel
statistical genetics methods on whole-genome ARGs will lead to faster, better-powered, and
more rigorous approaches for studying and understanding the genetics and evolution of
complex traits. The proposed methods can be directly applied to study human diseases and
enable new discoveries.

title: Training a new generation of vaccinologists
text:
The Emory VTP-T32 addresses the urgent need for training the next generation of vaccinologists. Vaccines have
dramatically reduced the burden of infectious diseases, shown great potential for preventing and controlling
conditions, and often are highly cost-effective. However, to achieve the full potential of vaccines and address
difficulties that have hindered progress, a new generation of well-prepared scientists continues to be needed.

title: Reactivation of developmental signaling programs during human injury-repair
text:
Several studies have demonstrated that during intestinal injury-repair and regeneration, a
primitive/developmental gene expression program is re-activated in the adult; however, all the data
supporting this phenomenon has been generated in mice. Using bulk and single-cell RNA-seq data
from in vivo and in vitro human developing and adult intestines, we have identified a gene signature
associated with the developing human intestine that includes the EGF family member, EPIREGULIN
(EREG) and found that multiple forms of injury in adult human organoids and in iPSC-derived
intestinal organoids transplanted into mice (in vivo-like organoids) induce these developmental genes.
We will mechanistically interrogate human injury-repair and regeneration by testing the hypothesis
that injury re-activates a developmental expression program, which requires EREG upregulation for
the appropriate functional tissue repair and regeneration.

title: Dissecting the mechanisms driving isoprenoid-dependent immune dysregulation in pathology of mevalonate kinase deficiency
text:
Mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD) is a rare inherited metabolic disorder characterized by a range of
symptoms, including autoinflammatory syndrome. This project seeks to provide a detailed analysis of the
immunological alterations that link MKD to the development of inflammation. Additionally, we will assess the
effects of supplementing metabolites that are deficient due to the metabolic defect on the immune changes
associated with the disease, with the potential to explore these interventions as treatment options.

title: Genetics and Genomics Training Grant
text:
The Duke University Program in Genetics and Genomics (UPGG) research training program
prepares predoctoral students for a variety of career paths in biomedical sciences. UPGG
students learn critical technical, operational and professional skills through the conduct of
genetics and genomics research while contributing to fundamental knowledge of basic biologic
processes as well as translational research impacting human health. Upon graduation, our
trainees will have a wide range of professional skills necessary to excel in biomedical research
at academic institutions, private industry, government agencies, and beyond.

title: Precursors of Anxiety: The Role of Lateralized Brain Activation and Maternal Sensitivity
text:
This study is aimed at increasing our understanding of etiological factors associated with the most frequently
occurring anxiety symptoms/disorders. Developmental shifts in fearful reactivity and the underlying
neurophysiology will be examined via an intensive longitudinal design, elucidating change-related effects
contributing to emergence of anxiety, and the influence of maternal sensitivity on these effects. Most salient
predictors of early anxiety symptoms represent targets for preventative efforts.

title: Cross-species Analysis of Bacterial Gene Networks
text:
Genes work in groups to dictate the properties and behaviors of bacteria, but which genes work together and
how they work is often unknown. To address these issues, we propose to study groups of genes and ask about
how they function together across multiple species of bacteria. Gene groups that function similarly across
species may reveal fundamental features of bacterial life and potentially serve as future antibiotic targets.

title: pan-XLSM: an AI-powered microscopy platform for imaging and analysis of highly expanded tissue samples
text:
Mapping the complexities of biological functions and disorders at the molecular level requires a
technology capable of visualizing the 3D distribution of molecular markers within tissues at the
nanoscale. In this project, we will develop pan-XLSM, the first automated three-dimensional
spatial biology platform for multiplexed protein imaging at ~20 nm resolution, and validate its
use in characterizing mitochondrial morphology disruptions in kidney, liver, and brain tissues.
This advancement is crucial for advancing public health, as it aims to revolutionize the analysis
of tissue architecture and cellular interactions, opening new possibilities for diagnosis,
treatment, and prevention in various fields of medicine.

title: Neural Computations Underlying Intensity Perception Across Sensory Systems
text:
All animals, including humans, navigate and interpret the world through the combined perception of a variety of
sensory stimuli. One fundamental feature of sensation is perceived intensity, which is the perceptual feature
describing magnitude of physical stimuli and is key to weight and compare stimuli both within and across sensory
modalities. The research proposed here tests the overall hypothesis that the intensity of olfactory and auditory
uni-modal and multi-modal stimuli is encoded on a common perceptual scale, whose neural underpinning is
implemented in the basolateral amygdala or orbitofrontal cortex.

title: Quantification of Tics in Tourette Syndrome
text:
Tourette Syndrome (TS) is a chronic neurodevelopmental disorder that is characterized by tics, which are
involuntary, repetitive movements and vocalizations. A major limitation in TS healthcare is the lack of clinical
assessment measures to objectively diagnose and quantify tics and their severity, one reason that many
individuals with TS go unrecognized or experience long delays in diagnosis and treatment access. In this
study, we will create a large video and questionnaire dataset of N = 1,000 individuals with tics, code the videos
for tic symptoms using human raters to better understand the spectrum of symptoms, and use the coded
videos to train a computer algorithm to automatically detect and quantify tics.

title: Testing health hazards from implementation of far-UVC irradiation as an intervention technology to reduce airborne disease transmission
text:
New intervention technology to reduce the transmission of airborne diseases is vital to improve public
health, and is especially needed within healthcare environments where workers are substantially more at risk
of becoming ill. Irradiation with far-UVC wavelengths, specifically from 200-230 nm, is a promising solution
which we have previously shown to be effective at inactivating airborne viruses and, unlike conventional UV
irradiation, has shown promise as being safe for human exposure. This work will test the biological effects of
far-UVC radiation upon the eyes and skin of mice; these results are necessary to evaluate health hazards from
exposure to these wavelengths and are critical for the adoption of this new technology.
